body: Standard campaign-level Target ROAS gives no control over individual bids, so on thin-demand days the algorithm can pay very high CPCs. Its example: an ecommerce advertiser on tROAS saw CPC spikes up to $25 on low-demand days; moving into a portfolio with a $9 max CPC put a guardrail on budget blowouts while leaving Smart Bidding room to pursue the ROAS goal. Portfolios also pool conversion data across campaigns with the same target (for example 700% ROAS across all non-brand campaigns), which speeds learning and lets budget shift to better performers. Do not put campaigns with different goals (clearance versus new arrivals) in one portfolio, or campaigns too low in volume to benefit. claim: Google Ads credits conversions to the click date, so the last 3 to 4 days always look weak; judge recent days with 'conversions (by conversion time)' columns.
body: By default, Google Ads attributes a conversion to the date of the ad click, not the date of the purchase. If someone clicks on the 1st and the 3rd and buys on the 7th, the sale is written back to the click dates. Most other platforms log it on the purchase date. The consequence: when you open the account, the trailing three to four days (often the trailing week) show low conversions and ROAS in every account, because clicks from those days have not yet had time to convert and be written back. Operators who do not know this react to a dip that is not real, change bids or budgets, and can start a genuine decline. The agency's fix is to add the 'by conversion time' versions of conversions, conversion value and ROAS as custom columns, which count conversions on the day they happened and give a usable read on the last few days. How to apply: before any diagnosis, switch to conversion-time columns or exclude the most recent days; check the account's typical conversion lag in the path or time-lag reports; and widen the date range to a period that holds enough conversions for the account's volume, rather than reacting to one day.

claim: In a Google Ads decline, apply targeted fixes before any rebuild; restructuring resets learning and can start a spiral of falling performance and bigger changes.
body: Every rebuild or major restructure in Google Ads triggers a learning reset, which lowers conversion rate while the system re-enters auctions. The agency describes a common spiral: performance drops, the buyer makes a big change, learning resets and performance drops further, prompting another big change. Its rule is to default to a fix, not a rebuild, and to move to a rebuild only when the available fixes cannot plausibly close the gap to historical performance. Within fixes, avoid the 'kitchen sink': if conversion rate fell and you change the offer, page design and ad copy at once, you may recover but never learn which change worked, and the next time you must throw everything at it again. Decide by severity: in a dire situation, apply many fixes together and accept that you will not know why; in a moderate dip, apply one or two high-impact fixes, give them time to read, then add more. Be honest about expected impact: a headline tweak will not rescue a business-level decline unless the headline change caused it. Final gate: do not touch the account until you can finish the sentence 'this campaign is underperforming because this metric dropped, driven by this sub-metric, caused by this trigger'.

claim: Treat CPC as near-vanity: CPA = CPC / conversion rate, so higher CPCs only matter when conversion rate does not rise with them.
body: When efficiency drops in Google Ads, the agency splits it with two formulas: CPA = CPC / conversion rate, and clicks = impressions x CTR. Causes of a bad CPC rise: quality score changes (add expected CTR, ad relevance and landing page experience as keyword columns and compare before and after the inflection date); a new competitor (compare auction insights before and after); or more aggressive bidding pushing into costlier auctions that do not pay back. Landing page experience is the slowest to fix: the agency has waited weeks to months for Google to re-crawl and re-score after site fixes. If clicks fall instead, check impression share lost to budget versus lost to rank: hitting the daily budget means budget is the limit; falling clicks and impressions without hitting budget point to bid and rank (quality score, competition, bidding). Conversion-rate drops: check tracking, then landing page changes (URL, price, redirects, merchandising, upsells), search-term mix, a learning reset, or an ended promotion or free-shipping change.

claim: Use a feeder structure: a Standard Shopping campaign at a very low target ROAS (around 50%) for cold reach plus a high-tROAS PMax (around 600%) converting warm traffic.
body: The agency describes a target-ROAS trap. A campaign trailing about 4.2x gets a 400% tROAS; it stabilizes; the buyer nudges the target up in steps until spend starts to pull back near 500% to 600%. ROAS on the same $1,000 a day now reads 5x or 6x and looks like great buying, but the higher target has narrowed the campaign to people already likely to buy, mostly warm and returning visitors, and new-customer acquisition has shrunk. One campaign, usually Standard Shopping, runs a very low target ROAS (as low as 50%, or 0.5x) and is allowed to reach everyone searching the relevant terms, including cold audiences. Big Flare separates them into different campaigns so each shows its own ROAS, gives brand a much higher target, gives non-brand a lower target because its sales are more incremental, and shifts budget toward non-brand if the account is over-weighted on brand. claim: A target ROAS set above what a campaign achieves shrinks its exploration to near zero and starts a death spiral; when spend falls, cut the target aggressively, not gradually.
body: Blue Sense Digital explains Google bidding as expansive versus restrictive. Maximise conversion value spends some budget, which they estimate at about 30%, on testing: new keywords, audiences, placements and regions that look adjacent but unproven, which is how it finds scale. A restrictive target ROAS set above the campaign's real ROAS (for example a 4.5 target on a campaign doing 4.0) leaves roughly 0% for testing, since every dollar must hit the target. The spiral: performance dips, the campaign misses the target, it narrows its audience and spends less, conversions fall (say from 100 to 80 in 30 days), the bidding model has less data from its 30 to 90-day lookback, targeting worsens, conversions fall further, and the campaign slowly dies. Leaving the target unchanged lets it die; nudging it down slowly does not stop it. Cut the target hard to restore volume. They also warn that maximise conversions (lowest CPA) pushes budget to cheap products: a $40 t-shirt at a $20 CPA wins over a $200 jumper at $60 CPA even when the jumper returns 3.5x versus 2x.
conditions: Google Shopping, PMax and Search campaigns on smart bidding with modest conversion volume; ecommerce catalogues with mixed price points.
fails_when: High-volume campaigns where the model has ample data; temporary dips from stockouts or seasonality that will recover without changing targets; brands that need hard efficiency floors for cash reasons.

claim: For ecommerce, keep about 80 to 90% of Google spend in Shopping rather than Search, because the image, price and title shown before the click filter for higher-intent visitors.
body: Blue Sense Digital's view is that search campaigns suit service businesses, while stores should put about 80 to 90% of Google spend into Shopping (standard Shopping or Performance Max). The reason is what the shopper sees before paying for the click. A search ad shows a headline, a description few read, and some extensions; for a query like 'red dress size medium for wedding' it can match the words but not show the style or price, so many clickers arrive, see the product and leave, at $1 to $2 a click. A Shopping ad shows the product image, price, title, brand, any promotion and reviews, so people who click have already accepted how it looks and what it costs. This matters most in visual categories such as fashion. Remaining search spend goes to brand defence where proven and to high-intent non-brand terms. body: Blue Sense Digital describes a client spending a few hundred thousand dollars a month on Performance Max when clicks suddenly soared and ROAS fell about 20%. In Gmail, PMax builds an email-style ad from your assets and feed; opening that 'email' counts as a click, so you get many cheap clicks (around 10 cents) that never reach the site. claim: Google Merchant Center bans promotional overlays, watermarks, borders and added logos on the main product image, sets a 500 x 500 minimum from 31 January 2027, recommends about 1500 x 1500.
body: Google Merchant Center bans promotional overlays, watermarks, borders and added logos on the main product image, sets a 500 x 500 minimum from 31 January 2027, recommends about 1500 x 1500, and wants the product to fill 75 to 90% of the frame. The Merchant Center image_link specification says the main product image must give a clean, unobstructed view of the exact item sold. Not allowed: promotional elements or overlays (calls to action, price or shipping details, promotional words, condition text), barcodes or QR codes over the photo, watermarks or copyright stamps, brand or retailer logos added in post-production unless physically on the product, placeholders or generic graphics, single-colour squares, borders, and products not sold together. Minimum size is 500 x 500 pixels from 31 January 2027; about 1500 x 1500 or larger is recommended; files up to 64 megapixels or 16 MB. It asks for one variant per image with its true colour, a product filling 75 to 90% of the image, stable URLs and extra angles in additional_image_link. So any sale badge, price sticker or frame belongs on an ad layer, never baked into the image the feed uses.
conditions: Products shown in Google Shopping, free listings and Performance Max via Merchant Center.
fails_when: Some categories have exceptions (hardware, vehicles and parts, some paint). Additional images are less strict than the main image.

claim: Google does not restrict rivals from bidding on your trademark as a keyword; it can restrict a rival's use of the trademark in ad text after the owner files a complaint.
body: Google's trademark policy says it will not restrict trademarks used as keywords. The policy looks at whether the trademark appears in the ad itself. Ads from a direct competitor that use the trademark in ad text, or that use it in a confusing or misleading way, can be restricted. Resellers and sellers of compatible parts may use the term if the landing page mainly sells those goods and shows prices, and the ad makes clear they are a reseller. Complaints go through Google's Report Content process, are limited to the countries and industries where the owner shows trademark rights, and name specific advertisers by URL. How to apply: a store cannot stop rivals bidding on its name, so it protects brand searches with its own brand campaign, and files a trademark complaint only for rivals that put its name in their ad text.
conditions: Google Ads Search and Shopping in markets where the store holds a registered or provable trademark.
fails_when: The store has no trademark rights in that country or industry; the rival uses a descriptive dictionary word that is also the brand name; Google changes its policy. This is not legal advice.

claim: Brand exclusions work on Search and Performance Max (Search and Shopping inventory); brand inclusions are Search only; one brand entry matches other spellings and languages.
body: Google's brand settings let a Search campaign serve only on queries tied to chosen brands (inclusions) or keep Search and Performance Max campaigns off queries tied to brands (exclusions). For Performance Max, exclusions cover Search and Shopping inventory. Brand lists use broad matching, so one entry matches other languages, scripts and common variants; brands that share no words need separate entries. Only brands in Google's library (logo, trademark, domain, dominant product name or business name) can be picked. Exclusions win over inclusions. Google warns that brand settings narrow reach and may lower performance, so use them only where needed. How to apply: exclude the store's own brand from Performance Max and non-brand Search, and run a separate brand campaign with exact-match brand keywords or a brand inclusion.

claim: Merchant Center needs the feed price to match the landing page price exactly; mismatches disapprove products and can lead to account suspension.
body: Googlebot compares the price attribute with the price in the page HTML and structured data. Prices must match exactly, in the same currency shown on the page; prices added by script after the page loads can trigger errors. Sale price dates and time zones must be right, and minimum-quantity items must show the total for that quantity. A product with a mismatch may be disapproved, and repeated mismatches may lead to account suspension. After the fix, Google re-crawls over the next hours or days and reapproves the product; a website check can be requested to speed this up. Scheduled feed fetches or the Merchant API keep prices current. How to apply: before any sale, schedule the feed update for the minute site prices change, and check that the page price sits in the HTML, not only in a script.
conditions: Google Merchant Center feeds for Shopping, Performance Max, Demand Gen product ads and free listings.
fails_when: Setting names and review times change; a native platform sync may already update prices fast enough for stores with rare price changes.

claim: Merchant Center titles may run 1 to 150 characters with the most important details first, since buyers often see only the first 70 or fewer; no promotional text or caps for emphasis.
body: Google's title specification allows 1 to 150 characters and truncates longer titles with a warning. It asks for the most important details first, because users usually notice only the first 70 or fewer characters depending on screen size. Include the product name, the brand where it sets the product apart, and variant details such as size or colour, and describe the same product as the landing page. Titles must not include promotional text (price, sale, shipping, delivery dates, company name), capital letters for emphasis, symbols, HTML, extra spaces or poorly understood foreign words. How to apply: rewrite feed titles so searched words sit in the first 70 characters, keep sale messages in their own attributes, and check every rewrite against this list before upload.

claim: A responsive search ad takes up to 15 headlines of 30 characters and 4 descriptions of 90 (minimum 3 and 2); Google advises against pinning for most advertisers and suggests 2 or 3 options per pinned slot.
body: Google's help page sets the limits: up to 15 headlines and 4 descriptions per responsive search ad, at least 3 headlines and 2 descriptions, 30 characters per headline, 90 per description and 15 per display path field. Korean, Japanese and Chinese characters count double. Pinning fixes a headline or description to one position; headline positions 1 and 2 and description position 1 always show, while headline 3 and description 2 may not. Google says pinning is not recommended for most advertisers and can lower ad strength; if every position is pinned, unpinned text never shows. Where pinning is needed, pin 2 or 3 different options to each pinned slot, and put text that must always appear (such as a required disclaimer) in headline 1, headline 2 or description 1. Google also advises as many unique headlines as possible, at least one keyword in headlines, first three headlines that work together, and at least two ads rated Good or Excellent per ad group. How to apply: write the full bank, pin only what must always show, and check every line stands alone in any order.
